Descriptive statistics summarized insomnia levels, and bivariate tests and multiple linear regression were used to examine group differences and predictors in SPSS. Results: The mean ISI score was 11.8 ± 5.3, indicating subthreshold insomnia among paramedic students. Higher insomnia severity was observed among single students than among married students (12.1 vs. 7.4, p = 0.005), among students at private universities (19.3 vs. 11.6, p = 0.001), and among those with chronic medical or diagnosed mental illness (p < 0.05). No significant differences were found by gender, region, academic level, or dormitory residence (p > 0.05). Regression analysis showed that marital status and university type were significant predictors of insomnia symptom severity. Conclusions: Insomnia is common among EMS students and may have implications for both student well-being and future clinical performance. Addressing sleep health within EMS education may support better academic outcomes and safer healthcare delivery.

papers.title: Bullying and Cyberbullying in Childhood and Adolescence: A Narrative Review and Proposed Clinical Response Framework.
papers.abstract: Existing reviews establish that bullying and cyberbullying are associated with substantial health burden, but they rarely integrate conceptual distinctions, evidence strength, and healthcare response. To synthesize evidence on traditional bullying, peer victimization, and cyberbullying among children and adolescents and to identify clinically defensible implications and research priorities. A structured narrative review informed by SANRA addressed three questions concerning construct boundaries, health consequences and modifiers, and healthcare response. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched through 29 August 2026; Google Scholar supported citation tracing and the retrieval of named institutional reports. Eligibility, selection, charting, and narrative evidence-characterization procedures are reported. The final synthesis included 61 sources (53 journal articles and eight institutional reports, guidance documents, or books). Cross-national surveillance estimated 11% repeated school bullying and 15% cybervictimization under different frequency thresholds. Meta-analytic estimates were 25% for victimization and 16% each for perpetration and bully-victim involvement. A longitudinal meta-analysis of 27 studies (13,497 participants) found a small prospective association between cybervictimization and later mental-health symptoms. School programs reduced perpetration by approximately 18-19% and victimization by 15-16%; cyberbullying effects were small (g = -0.18 and -0.13, respectively). The evidence was strongest for associations with internalizing symptoms, suicidality, psychosomatic complaints, sleep disruption, and impaired functioning but bidirectionality and residual confounding limit causal inference. Symptom- or risk-triggered, behavior-specific inquiry and coordinated safety assessment are justified; evidence is insufficient to recommend universal clinical screening. BV-CARE is presented as an author-developed, hypothesis-generating framework requiring stakeholder co-design, feasibility testing, and prospective validation before routine use.

papers.title: Experiences and Perceptions of Older Adults Participating in Physical Exercise, Cognitive Training, and Health Education Programs: A Qualitative Study Nested in a Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Background: Multimodal interventions combining physical exercise and cognitive stimulation may improve sleep and healthy aging among older adults. However, little is known about how participants experience these interventions. This study explored the experiences and perceptions of older adults who participated in physical exercise, combining physical exercise and cognitive training, or health education programs designed to improve sleep. Methods: A qualitative process evaluation using reflexive thematic analysis was conducted following a randomized controlled trial in Toledo, Spain. Twenty-one community-dwelling adults aged ≥65 years from the control, physical exercise (Otago), and combined exercise plus CogniFit® groups completed semistructured interviews. The interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed from the recordings, and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The study was reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guidelines. Results: Six themes emerged: participation experience, perceived changes in sleep, benefits beyond sleep, evaluation of program components, facilitators and barriers, and maintenance of healthy habits. The participants reported high levels of satisfaction across all the groups. Beyond perceived changes in sleep, participants described perceived benefits related to physical well-being, cognitive stimulation, social interaction, and healthier habits. The participants also identified facilitators and barriers affecting engagement and maintenance. Exercise was valued for its simplicity and adaptability, whereas cognitive training was considered stimulating despite initial technological challenges. The main barriers were preexisting health conditions and difficulties using digital technology. Many participants intended to maintain the healthy habits acquired during the intervention. Conclusions: The participants who completed the qualitative interviews generally described positive experiences across the three groups. These findings provide insights relevant to the design of person-centered and accessible interventions and highlight factors that may influence engagement and maintenance in community settings.

papers.title: Perceived Changes in Psychological Well-Being, Cognitive Domains, and Sleep Quality Among Jordanian Adults Observing Ramadan Intermittent Fasting: A Prospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Ramadan intermittent fasting (RIF) involves significant shifts in sleep patterns and circadian rhythms that may affect neurological health. This study aimed to evaluate changes in neuropsychiatric and neurocognitive functions in relation to sleep quality among healthy adults observing RIF. Methods: We recruited healthy adults from various regions in Jordan for this prospective cohort study. We used validated self-report questionnaires to assess mental health and sleep parameters. Anxiety and depression were assessed using the GAD-7 and PHQ-9, respectively. We measured resilience using the 10-item Nicholson McBride Resilience Questionnaire (NMRQ), and the Neuro-QoL (cognitive functions domain) assessed memory and attention. We assessed sleep quality using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). We administered all tools before (BR) and at the end of Ramadan (DR) to track changes in symptom severity and functional status. Results: A total of 723 healthy adults (mean age: 28.82 ± 12.04 years) completed both assessments. A paradoxical divergence emerged between mood and sleep parameters: mean scores for depression (PHQ-9: 8.65 to 7.70) and anxiety (GAD-7: 6.75 to 5.65; both p = 0.0001) improved significantly, with a higher proportion of participants reporting minimal symptoms during Ramadan. Conversely, overall sleep quality (PSQI) deteriorated markedly, with the percentage of participants classified as having "good sleep quality" dropping from 66.4% to 34.9% (p = 0.0001). While sleep latency and sleep disturbances improved slightly, subjective sleep quality and sleep duration worsened significantly (p ≤ 0.01). Additionally, Neuro-QoL cognitive scores decreased from 30.60 to 28.97 (p = 0.0001), whereas total resilience scores remained stable (p = 0.897). Conclusions: RIF is associated with significant improvements in depression and anxiety scores despite a concurrent deterioration in overall sleep quality and duration. While these findings suggest a favorable impact on subjective mental well-being, the observational design precludes establishing causal relationships. This paradoxical interplay between fasting-induced mood enhancements and sleep disruptions highlights the need for future prospective studies utilizing objective measurement tools.

papers.title: Two seconds per day: Limitations of circadian burden metrics in the Permanent Daylight Saving Time debate.
A motivational model of sleep disturbance in winter athletes: the roles of motivational climate, basic psychological needs, and burnout.
papers.abstract: The present research investigated the associations among motivational climates, basic psychological needs, burnout, and sleep disturbance in winter sports athletes guided by achievement goal theory and self-determination theory. It included 456 participants (263 males, 193 females, aged 18 to 25 years) from three sports universities across five winter sports events. Participants completed four psychological scales related to the study variables. The results indicated that task-involving climate was positively associated with basic psychological needs satisfaction, whereas ego-involving climate showed a negative association. In turn, basic psychological needs satisfaction was negatively related to burnout, which was positively associated with sleep disturbance. Overall, these findings underscore the sequential associations linking motivational climates, basic psychological needs, burnout, and sleep disturbance within a coherent motivational process model, supporting the inclusion of sleep disturbance as an outcome in the motivational model.

papers.title: Symptom improvement with dosing above 9 g of low-sodium oxybate: effectiveness and safety in participants with narcolepsy in the DUET study.
papers.abstract: Evaluate effectiveness/safety of low-sodium oxybate (LXB; Xywav®) dosages > 9 g/night in participants with narcolepsy (type 1 [NT1] or 2 [NT2]). Jazz DUET (prospective, multiple-cohort, open-label study [NCT05875974]) included screening, 9-day baseline (LXB 9 g/night ["LXB 9 g BL"]), 2-8-week titration, 2-week stable-dose, 9-day end-of-treatment (LXB > 9 g- ≤ 12 g ["optimized LXB > 9 g EOT"]; twice-nightly, first/second max doses = 7.5/4.5 g), and 2-week follow-up. Endpoints included Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Narcolepsy Severity Scale-clinical trials version (NSS-CT), Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S) and Change (PGI-C), and polysomnography (PSG)-measured respiratory assessments. Forty-eight participants took LXB > 9 g/night (mean ± SD age: 39.2 ± 10.9 years; 62.5% female); 44 (NT1, n = 28; NT2, n = 16) completed the study. Mean ± SD stable-LXB dosage (n = 45) was 11.1 ± 1.0 g/night (most common [43.8%], 12 g/night). From LXB 9 g BL to optimized LXB > 9 g EOT, mean ± SE ESS scores (11.4 ± 0.8 to 8.3 ± 0.9), NSS-CT (NT1) scores (17.3 ± 2.2 to 9.4 ± 2.1), and NSS-2-CT (NT2) scores (9.7 ± 1.7 to 4.3 ± 1.6) improved. Fewer participants rated their disease as severe (61.4% to 29.5%), and most (92.3%) reported their disease improved. AHI (1.8 ± 0.4 to 1.6 ± 0.3), CAI (0.01 ± 0.01 to 0.01 ± 0.00), and mean SpO2 (95.8 ± 0.2 to 95.8 ± 0.1) remained stable. Common TEAEs included nausea (12.5%), vomiting (12.5%), and headache (10.4%). Participants taking LXB > 9 g/night experienced further improvements in narcolepsy symptoms versus 9 g/night, suggesting some patients may require higher dosages for optimal benefit. No changes in mean respiratory PSG measures were observed. TEAEs align with the known safety profile. Findings support individualized clinical decision-making with higher LXB dosages. Trial name: A Study to Investigate the Effect of XYWAV on Sleepiness, Polysomnography, and Functional Outcomes in Participants With Idiopathic Hypersomnia or Narcolepsy; URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05875974 ; ID number: NCT05875974. Narcolepsy is a heterogeneous disorder requiring individualized treatment strategies to optimize symptom management. This study fills a critical knowledge gap by evaluating effectiveness and safety of low-sodium oxybate (LXB) dosing regimens higher (> 9-12 g/night) than the recommended dosage (6-9 g/night). Participants with narcolepsy taking LXB > 9 g/night experienced further overall symptom benefit compared with 9 g/night at baseline, suggesting some patients may require higher dosages to achieve optimal therapeutic benefit. The safety profile, including respiratory safety parameters, was comparable to that observed at 9 g/night. Findings demonstrate that LXB can be utilized at dosages up to 12 g/night to optimize effectiveness, supporting individualized clinical decision-making. Low-sodium oxybate (LXB; Xywav®) is a medication used to treat narcolepsy symptoms. The recommended dosage range is 6 g to 9 g/night, but it has been reported that some people take higher dosages (greater than 9 g/night). This study was the first to evaluate higher dosages of LXB (greater than 9 g/night and up to 12 g/night). Before this study, these higher dosages had not been formally studied. This study was done to evaluate whether higher dosages improve narcolepsy symptoms and/or impact side effects. LXB is a central nervous system depressant, so there was a need to see if higher dosages could impact breathing during sleep. The study enrolled people who were already taking LXB at 9 g/night (the highest recommended dose) and who clinicians thought could benefit from higher dosages. While taking LXB 9 g/night, participants completed tests to measure their symptoms. Participants then worked with a clinician for 2 to 8 weeks to find a higher LXB dosage that worked best for them. The highest dosage allowed was 12 g/night. By the end of the study, the average dosage taken was 11.1 g/night, and almost half (44%) of participants were taking 12 g/night. Once participants found their ideal dosage, they stayed on this dosage for 2 weeks. Then, they repeated the same tests that they completed before. Forty-eight participants started the study. Forty-four completed the study. With higher LXB dosages (compared to 9 g/night), participants on average had less excessive daytime sleepiness, fewer cataplexy attacks, and less severe narcolepsy symptoms. At the beginning of the study when taking LXB 9 g/night, most participants (61.4%) said their disease was severe. After taking higher dosages, this dropped to 29.5%. At the end of the study, nearly all (92.3%) said their overall disease improved with higher dosages. Nobody said their disease worsened. In general, higher dosages did not worsen breathing during sleep. The most common side effects were nausea, vomiting, and headache. These side effects are similar to what is commonly experienced with lower dosages. This study shows that LXB treatment can be adjusted for each person. Higher dosages (>9-12 g/night) may help some patients find further improvement in their narcolepsy symptoms.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine

papers.title: Six-month comparative outcomes of endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty versus laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy: an MBSAQIP analysis.
papers.abstract: North American data regarding long-term efficacy and durability of endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) are remarkably scarce outside of clinical trial settings hampering our understanding of its optimal role in the obesity care continuum. The aims of this study are to compare safety and efficacy of elective ESG versus laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) at 6 months using accredited MBSAQIP centers. Data were obtained from the Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery Accreditation and Quality Improvement Program (MBSAQIP) database for 2023 and merged with the 6‑month follow‑up data file. The primary objectives of the study were to characterize the long-term six-month changes in weight and metabolic comorbidities of ESG patients in contrast to their LSG counterparts. Logistic regression models were to evaluate for differences in six-month serious complications and emergency department readmissions between ESG and LSG. A total of 115,476 patients were included, comprising 114,967 LSG and 509 ESG procedures. Patients undergoing ESG were slightly older (44.5 ± 11.2 vs. 42.4 ± 11.9 years, p = 0.0001) and had lower baseline BMI (40.9 ± 8.6 vs. 45.0 ± 7.8 kg/m2, p < 0.0001) and mean body weight (113.2 ± 28 vs. 124.5 ± 26.3 kg). At 6 months, LSG resulted in greater weight reduction, with larger BMI loss (8.2 ± 10.8 vs. 3.9 ± 12.0 kg/m2, p < 0.0001), and total weight loss (22.6 ± 35.6 vs. 11.1 ± 37.7 kg, p < 0.0001). For patients undergoing LSG, there was a near 50% reduction in medication/insulin-dependent diabetes along with improvements in rates of dyslipidemia, hypertension, and sleep apnea. Importantly, no clinically meaningful comorbidity improvements from baseline to 6 months were seen following ESG. When compared to ESG at 6 months, LSG provides an improvement in total body weight loss, has a reduced operative time, and is associated with dramatic metabolic comorbidity improvement including a reduction in resolution of medication and insulin-dependent diabetes. No clinically meaningful comorbidity resolution was seen in patients receiving ESG compared to LSG at 6 months although this cohort was less comorbid at baseline.

papers.title: Quantitative assessment of liver regenerative potential during accelerated aging: regenerative reserve and regenerative status indices.
papers.abstract: Age-related changes in hepatocyte ploidy, binucleation, proliferative activity, and senescence-associated cell-cycle arrest may jointly influence liver regenerative capacity, but these features are usually evaluated separately. We developed two composite indices and examined their behavior in a long-term rat model of chronic circadian disruption. Male Wistar rats were assigned to control lighting, constant illumination (dark deprivation; DD), or constant illumination with melatonin (DD + melatonin, 10 mg/kg five times weekly) and assessed at 6, 12, 18, and 24 months. The Index of Regenerative Reserve (IRR) was defined as the proportion of binucleated hepatocytes divided by mean hepatocyte ploidy. The Integrated Index of Regenerative Status (IRS) further incorporated Ki-67 (a marker of active cell proliferation) and p21 (a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor associated with cell-cycle arrest) as fractional terms: IRS = IRR × (1 + Ki-67)/(1 + p21).In DD animals, IRR declined from 2.00 ± 0.42 at 6 months to 0.386 ± 0.19 at 24 months; the corresponding 24-month IRS was 0.32 ± 0.17. In DD + melatonin animals, 24-month IRR and IRS were 2.285 ± 0.41 and 2.08 ± 0.16, respectively. Exploratory receiver-operating-characteristic analysis yielded areas under the curve of 0.843 for IRR and 0.905 for IRS. These findings support IRR and IRS as experimental composite descriptors of the hepatic regenerative phenotype. External validation and direct functional regeneration assays are required before broader biological or clinical interpretation.

papers.title: Task-specific theta enhancement and domain-general alpha/beta suppression as oscillatory signatures of cognitive flexibility.
papers.abstract: Cognitive flexibility-the ability to adapt to changing situational or task demands-is a fundamental aspect of human cognition and a potential source of individual differences in higher-order cognitive abilities. To further understand the neural mechanisms underlying this ability, we examined event-related spectral perturbations (ERSP) in three cued switching tasks (parity/magnitude, global/local, number/letter) in a sample of 148 adults. Employing a data-driven approach that combined mass-univariate time-frequency analysis, cluster-based permutation testing, and latent change structural equation modeling, we identified two robust neural signatures: a transient frontal theta increase and a sustained alpha/beta suppression. Both effects were more pronounced in switch compared to repeat trials. Frontal theta reflected task-specific control processes, whereas parietal alpha/beta indexed domain-general attentional processes that persisted from cue onset through target processing-consistent with two-stage models of task switching. Notably, flexibility-related alpha/beta dynamics did not correlate with measures of intelligence or working memory capacity. However, stronger cue-elicited alpha/beta suppression correlated with reduced non-decision-time switch costs, indicating more effective task preparation, underscoring that alpha/beta suppression captures a neurally coherent but behaviorally distinct dimension of cognitive flexibility. These findings provide evidence that alpha/beta suppression constitutes a reliable, cross-task generalizable neural signature of attentional reconfiguration during task switching, while highlighting the multi-component nature of individual differences in cognitive flexibility.

papers.title: A half-center oscillator regulates sleep pressure.
papers.abstract: Changes in oscillatory neural dynamics reflect-but may not necessarily determine-transitions between sleep stages and variations in sleep pressure. Here we show that sleep-control neurons innervating the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila (dFBNs) produce slow-wave activity (SWA) that is causally linked to sleep. The dFBN ensemble contains bistable cells whose membrane voltages oscillate between hyperpolarized DOWN and depolarized UP states. The oscillations rely on interhemispheric competition of two half-centers connected by inhibitory glutamatergic synapses. dFBN-restricted interference with glutamate release disrupts SWA and baseline as well as rebound sleep, whereas the optogenetic replay of SWA induces sleep. dFBNs generate SWA throughout the sleep-wake cycle (despite mutual antagonism with arousing dopaminergic neurons) and adjust its power to sleep need via sleep history-dependent increases in excitability and homeostatic synaptic depression. The oscillatory format permits a continuous encoding of sleep pressure but requires mechanisms that convert the amplitude-modulated signal into binary sleep-wake states.

papers.title: Topology-enhanced machine learning for speech signal processing.
papers.abstract: In artificial-intelligence-aided signal processing, existing deep learning models often exhibit a black-box structure. Here, conceptually beyond spectral analysis, we demonstrate that topological methods not only effectively capture intrinsic and complex structural information but can also enhance neural networks. We provide a transparent methodology, TopCap, to capture topological features inherent in time series for basic machine learning. Compared to prior approaches, we obtain descriptors that probe finer information such as the vibration of a time series. Notably, in classifying voiced and voiceless consonants, TopCap achieves an accuracy consistently standing in comparison with neural network models. Moreover, by integrating TopCap features into those neural networks, our approach improves upon state-of-the-art methods in terms of robustness against noise, as well as accuracy, stability, convergence of loss function, and interpretability.

papers.title: Slow Frontal Spindle Activity and Declarative Memory Retention During Daytime Naps.
papers.abstract: Memory consolidation refers to how newly encoded memories are strengthened and retained over time, and ample evidence indicates that sleep supports this process for both procedural and declarative memories. Although sleep spindles during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep have been associated with consolidation, it remains unclear whether all spindle types contribute equally. Spindles vary in frequency and topography, slow spindles (≤ 12.5 Hz) predominating frontally, fast spindles (> 12.5 Hz) parietally and recent work suggests that procedural memory consolidation relates to the temporal organization of spindles in 'trains' (events occurring < 6 s apart). We investigated whether a similar mechanism operates for declarative memory during daytime naps. Participants (Nap, N = 23; No-Nap, N = 15) completed an object-location task involving 36 item-location associations, tested immediately after learning and again following a 90-min nap opportunity or an equivalent wake period. The Nap group exhibited significantly better delayed memory, measured by combined recall-associative recognition scores and a greater proportion of nappers maintained or improved performance. Within the Nap group, memory was positively associated with local spindle density at frontal and parietal sites and with the proportion of slow frontal spindles clustered in trains during NREM2. Contrary to our expectations, however, these associations did not reach significance under two-tailed testing, possibly reflecting the limited sample size and thus lack of statistical power for an experimental design based on naps. Together, our results demonstrate a robust behavioural benefit of daytime naps for declarative memory retention and, more tentatively, point to slow frontal spindle activity as a candidate correlate for future work.

papers.title: Erratum to "The development quality of generic sleep questionnaires: A systematic review and call for action" [Sleep Med Rev 90 102362].
Scalp EEG and Intrinsic Optical Signal Imaging for Noninvasive Detection of Spreading Depolarizations in the Rat Cortex.
papers.abstract: Spreading depolarization (SD) is a slowly propagating wave of massive neuronal and glial depolarization in the cerebral cortex that occurs in various brain diseases. However, noninvasive SD detection remains challenging. Here, we used scalp EEG and intrinsic optical signal (IOS) recordings in rats of both sexes to assess the feasibility of noninvasively detecting high-potassium-induced SDs in the cortex. Scalp EEG failed to detect DC-shifts but revealed a characteristic SD-related depression of AC-EEG activity, while concurrent infrared IOS recordings captured reliable SD-associated signals. Although the magnitudes of AC-EEG depression and IOS signals during scalp recordings were several times smaller than those recorded epidurally, both techniques enabled high-fidelity SD detection. These findings demonstrate that noninvasive monitoring of scalp EEG and infrared IOS imaging reliably detects SDs in the rat cerebral cortex.

papers.title: Evaluating a CBT-I Intervention in Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Background: Insomnia negatively impacts quality of life and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Although national guidelines recommend cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), providers serving those 65 years of age and over may not have the expertise or resources to provide this treatment option. Objective: This study aimed to implement a brief online group CBT-I to adults 65 years of age and over, consisting of 4-week, 1-hour CBT-I classes at a virtual practice. Methods: The Insomnia Severity Index questionnaire was used to assess insomnia. A sleep diary was used to record an individual's quality and quantity of sleep to understand sleep patterns. A satisfaction survey was used to collect feedback on providers' experiences and perceptions during this quality improvement project. Results: The 17 patients evaluated had a mean CBT-I score of 22.53 (standard deviation [SD] = 2.57) preintervention and 14.88 (SD = 3.01) postintervention (t[16] = 10.51, p < .001). The mean difference of 7.65 (95% confidence interval [6.11, 9.18]) indicated a substantial reduction in insomnia symptoms. The effect size was large, with a Cohen's d of 2.48, indicating a strong impact of the intervention on reducing insomnia symptoms. Conclusions: A brief cognitive behavioral intervention for patients with insomnia in a practice serving those 65 years of age and over is feasible. Additional studies are needed to determine whether this type of intervention can be used to improve patient care or patient outcomes at other practices serving older adults.Implementation of nurse-supported cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) in primary care practices serving older adults may reduce insomnia severity and improve health-related quality of life through individualized education, behavioral guidance, and ongoing support.

papers.title: Assessing Behavioral and Environmental Facets of Obesity Unobtrusively Utilizing Digital Tools: Introducing the BETTER4U Indicators.
papers.abstract: Understanding obesity involves evaluating numerous contributing factors. Collecting the necessary data for this can impose a significant burden on both research participants during clinical studies and real-life deployments of digital tools aiding obesity management. The BETTER4U project (European Union's Horizon Europe, Grant Agreement ID 101080117) introduces 36 behavioral and 9 living environment indicators designed to unobtrusively and efficiently capture daily life through passive monitoring using market-available smartphones and smartwatches while accounting for environmental confounders. This concise set, intended for dietitians, physical activity experts, and healthcare professionals as a standard for assessing obesity-related behavior, summarizes the behavioral and environmental profile of a person with obesity/overweight. We present the selected indicators, their selection and implementation methodology and the high-level plan for their verification, describing their conceptual foundations and technical realization. These indicators can be deployed in a modular framework: by transforming raw sensor data into structured, interpretable measures they provide a scalable foundation for long-term monitoring of obesogenic behaviors, individual assessment, and evaluation of interventions targeting physical activity, diet, stress, and sleep. The indicators are intended for an expert-facing dashboard within the BETTER4U Intervention Platform, a participant-side interface within the BETTER4U application, and as input to the BETTER4U AI-based causal model, supporting relationship modeling between behavior, environment, and obesity outcomes to inform personalized interventions. This work lays the basis for data-driven validation of these indicators following the "BETTER4ALL Pilot Study" (ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT07120802), ahead of their use in the BETTER4U RCT among individuals with obesity/overweight.
authors: of the BETTER4U consortium, Project Coordinator George Dedoussis
papers.journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity

papers.title: Exploring emotion identification and categorisation in simulated central vision loss: an event-related potential study.
Exploring the prevalence of risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea in women.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a major risk factor for several medical conditions and poor quality of life. The objective of the study was to conduct an exploratory study to assess the prevalence of risk factors related to OSA in the adult female population seeking health care treatment at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, Escuela Nacional de Estudios Superiores (ENES) Unidad León. A cross-sectional study was conducted in 151 female patients using the STOP-BANG questionnaire with items related to snoring, fatigue, tiredness, sleepiness during the day, breathing interruptions, body mass index, age, neck circumference, and sex. Regarding age, 87.5% of females who presented sleep-related breathing disorders symptoms (p = 0.031) and 72.8% of females who woke up with fatigue (p = 0.002) were < 50 years old. However, females over 50 years with a neck circumference > 41 cm were 3.0 times more likely to experience fatigue, tiredness, and sleepiness during the daytime due to possible OSA. Snoring was not significantly associated with OSA risk factors; and female with a body mass index (BMI) > 35 kg/m2, representing a 6.4 times greater likelihood of experiencing sleep-related breathing disorders due to OSA. Within the limitations of this study, we confirmed that women < 50 years old reported greater fatigue and more sleep-related breathing disorders symptoms; and females with a high BMI also showed a higher risk of developing OSA.

papers.title: Sinonasal and Olfactory Quality of Life Following Endonasal Transsphenoidal Surgery for Pituitary Adenoma: A Multicenter Prospective Cohort Triphasic Recovery Analysis in Ethiopia.
papers.abstract: To characterize the sinonasal and olfactory quality of life (QoL) trajectory. A multicenter prospective cohort study was conducted on 91 patients undergoing TSS at Addis Ababa University teaching hospitals between May 2024 and August 2025. QoL was evaluated using the Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22) questionnaire v4 preoperatively and at 3- and 6-month postoperatively. Analysis revealed a characteristic triphasic recovery pattern: low preoperative baseline, a transient peak in morbidity at 3 months, and an improvement toward baseline by 6 months for most systemic domains. At 3 months, significant score worsening occurred for loss of smell/taste (mean: 1.7, p < 0.001), thick discharge (mean: 1.0, p < 0.001), congestion (mean: 1.0, p < 0.001), postnasal discharge (mean: 0.7, p < 0.001), and runny nose (mean: 0.5, p = 0.003). By 6 months, persistence was confined to loss of smell/taste (p < 0.001), thick discharge (p < 0.001), and congestion (p = 0.005). Exploratory analysis in the nasoseptal flap cohort (n = 3) showed higher scores. Preliminary findings of delayed ear pain/fullness in acromegaly at 6 months hypothesized to reflect a link between growth hormone normalization and altered Eustachian tube function. Poorer sleep with binostril access (p = 0.017) speculatively associated with bilateral synechiae under limited postoperative care. Unlike Western cohorts, protracted recovery may reflect lack of standardized high-volume saline irrigation and scheduled debridement. TSS demonstrates a favorable long-term QoL profile; however, localized sinonasal and olfactory deficits often persist at 6 months.

papers.title: A GRAPH CONVOLUTION BASED DUAL-BRANCH NETWORK FOR DECODING OF UPPER-LIMB MOTOR IMAGERY EEG SIGNALS.
papers.abstract: Analysing motor imagery EEG signals using conventional Euclidean feature computation is challenging due to low spatial resolution, non-stationarity, and complex inter-channel dependencies, which limit robust subject-independent generalization in brain-computer interface systems. This study proposes a graph-based convolutional framework for subject-independent decoding of upper-limb motor imagery. The model integrates graph convolution with skip connections and handcrafted time-frequency features, together with parallel spatial and temporal convolutional pathways. Graph convolution captures functional connectivity between electrodes, while convolutional modules enhance spatial-temporal representation learning. Subject-independent evaluation is ensured using Stratified Group K-Fold (SGKF) and Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) validation protocols. The framework was evaluated on the PhysioNet, BCI IV-2a, and BCI IV-2b datasets using multiple electrode configurations. For the PhysioNet dataset, three upper-limb classes were considered, achieving SGKF accuracies of 86.42%, 91.01%, and 93.91% using 64, 21, and 5 electrodes, respectively, and LOSO accuracies of 92.25%, 95.72%, and 96.01%. On the BCI IV-2a dataset, SGKF accuracies of 86.13%, 89.01%, and 92.33% were obtained, with LOSO accuracies reaching 97.12% using five electrodes. For the BCI IV-2b dataset, accuracies of 88.60% (SGKF) and 93.35% (LOSO) were achieved using only three electrodes. The proposed graph-based framework demonstrates competitive performance to representative graph-based methods while requiring fewer trainable parameters and EEG electrodes. These findings demonstrate that graph-based deep learning enables accurate, subject-independent motor imagery decoding with reduced model complexity and minimal electrode usage, supporting practical and resource-efficient brain-computer interface systems.

papers.title: Task-evoked brain network dynamics underlying executive function in preadolescent children.
papers.abstract: Executive function (EF) has been studied using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) based functional connectivity (FC); however, electroencephalography (EEG) based dynamic FC interactions supporting EF in children and explaining behavioral performance remain underexplored. We used EEG to examine FC within and between seven core brain networks: Default Mode (DMN), Dorsal Attention (DAN), Ventral Attention (VAN), Somatomotor (SMN), Frontoparietal (FPN), Visual (VIN), and Limbic (LIN), during a modified Eriksen flanker task. We aimed to identify dynamic network configurations linked to EF, specifically selective attention and inhibitory control in preadolescent children (8-10 years). Secondary analyses of source-localized EEG data from 84 children (mean age 8.89 ± 0.82 years; 51.2% female) were conducted. A Hidden Markov model extracted spatiotemporal dynamics, quantifying within- and between-network FC correlations. Support vector regression (SVR) with an interpretable kernel identified connectivity patterns predicting behavioral outcomes, including accuracy and reaction time (RT) interference. SVR moderately predicted Accuracy Interference (RMSE = 6.51, R2 = 0.48) and RT Interference (RMSE = 31.42, R2 = 0.26). Behavioral performance indices were most strongly associated with interference within VAN, DMN, SMN, and VIN. Notably, within-VAN FC explained between-subject variability in both Accuracy Interference (ρ = -0.28, p = 0.012) and RT Interference (r = 0.26, p = 0.017). Dynamic, task-based FC, particularly within-VAN, underpins individual differences in EF among preadolescent children. Stronger within-VAN reconfiguration during high cognitive demand trials supported accuracy but at the cost of slower responses, highlighting a trade-off between stability and efficiency in developing EF.
papers.journal: International journal of psychophysiology : official journal of the International Organization of Psychophysiology

papers.title: A comprehensive review of the neurobehavioral and neurotoxic effects of 6PPD-Q in fish, rodents, and humans.
papers.abstract: N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine (6PPD) is a widely used tire additive that undergoes environmental transformation to 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), which is ubiquitously detected in environmental matrices. Increasing evidence demonstrates that exposure to 6PPD-Q adversely affects organisms through neurobehavioral disruption and neurotoxicity. While studies document behavioral abnormalities and molecular alterations, a comprehensive synthesis linking these outcomes remains limited. The objective of this review was to synthesize current literature reporting neurobehavioral and neurotoxic effects of 6PPD-Q in fish, rodents, and humans using experimental and computational approaches. Using PRISMA guidelines, a search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar using several key phrases related to 6PPD-Q and neurotoxicity, capturing 1874 records. Relevant articles were assessed by full-text review for criteria eligibility, and the final review included 27 articles. In fish, exposure to 6PPD-Q can alter neurobehaviors like locomotor activity, anxiety-like responses, social and aggressive behaviors, and disturbances in circadian-regulated activities. Such behavioral outcomes correspond closely with neurotransmitter imbalance, neuroendocrine disruption, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and transcriptome changes affecting neural signaling pathways. In rodents, repeated or chronic exposure to 6PPD-Q leads to neuronal damage, cognitive impairment, anxiety-like behavior, and memory deficits. Human biomonitoring and mechanistic studies further associate 6PPD-Q exposure with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and molecular responses relevant to neurological diseases. Leveraging the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database, computational analysis revealed entities associated with 6PPD-Q in the database were related to Alzheimer's disease, dopaminergic synapses, neurotrophin signaling pathways, and Parkinson's disease. Taken together, data suggests that 6PPD-Q may interfere with neuronal signaling, connectivity, and plasticity, leading to behavioral deficits. Based on predictive docking scores using fish, rodent, and human orthologs, 6PPD-Q may interact with tyrosine hydroxylase and L-dopa decarboxylase which can potentially lead to disrupted dopamine biosynthesis pathways. Given the widespread environmental presence of 6PPD-Q and its continuous introduction into aquatic ecosystems, characterizing such mechanisms is critical for improving ecological and human health risk assessments.

papers.title: Ubiquitin-Like protein UBL1 orchestrates monocyte recruitment and pro-inflammatory macrophage activation in critical limb ischemia: Involving SUMOylation and stabilization of PER1.
papers.abstract: Critical limb ischemia (CLI), a severe manifestation of peripheral artery disease (PAD), is marked by accumulation of pro-inflammatory monocytes (Mos) and macrophages (Mφs) in ischemic skeletal muscles. Ubiquitin-Like Protein UBL1, an effector of small ubiquitin-like modifier mediated modification (SUMOylation), has been implicated in Mo/Mφ-associated tissue inflammation. However, the role of UBL1 in CLI has not been fully investigated. In this study, UBL1 expression was downregulated in peripheral blood Mos from CLI patients, and from hind limb ischemia (HLI) mice induced by femoral artery ligation (FAL). Adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated UBL1 knockdown (KD) in HIL mice hindered blood flow recovery, aggravated tissue injury, and induced pro-inflammatory Mφ activation. Moreover, UBL1 KD reduced period circadian regulator 1 (PER1) expression in peripheral blood Mos isolated from HLI mice. UBL1 promoted PER1 SUMOylation at lysine 146 (K146) site, thereby enhancing its protein stability. Hypoxia significantly inhibited this process, with ubiquitin conjugating enzyme E2 I (UBE2I) being critically involved. Additionally, UBL1 KD promoted hypoxia-induced Mo migration via C-C Chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2) signaling and advanced pro-inflammatory cytokine release from hypoxic THP-1 derived Mφs. More importantly, rescue assays demonstrated that PER1 mediated UBL1 KD-induced Mo migration and pro-inflammatory Mφ activation. In summary, this study highlights the significance of UBL1 in HLI via regulating PER1 SUMOylation.

papers.title: Automation in sleep state classification and maturity evaluation of EEG in preterm-born infants.
papers.abstract: There is a growing need to automate EEG monitoring of preterm-born infants, particularly where expert evaluation is limited. However, existing models necessitate human intervention for comprehensive assessment, thereby limiting the clinical applicability. We collected 165 EEG records from 65 preterm-born infants. 8-channel EEG records were segmented every 30second and allocated into eight classes (three preterm-equivalent, four term-equivalent, and one noise class). We performed noise detection, sleep state classification, and maturity assessment through the classification. ImageNet pretrained ResNet-50 was finetuned to classify the segmented EEG images. A novel index, named "maturity rate," was calculated as the proportion of term-equivalent labels in each EEG recording. The model achieved a macro F1 score of 0.58 and Cohen's Kappa of 0.58 for the 8-class classification. When the labels were merged into active sleep, quiet sleep, and noise categories, performance improved to an F1 score of 0.84 and Kappa of 0.74. The maturity rate increased continuously with postmenstrual age at the time of recording, reflecting functional brain development beyond the term-preterm dichotomy. Our model enables end-to-end EEG assessment of sleeping newborns by simultaneously performing noise detection, sleep state classification, and maturity assessment, with minimal need for human intervention.

papers.title: 24-Hour Movement Behavior Reallocations and Glycemic Variability in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Longitudinal Isotemporal Substitution Analysis.
papers.abstract: Background: Glycemic variability (GV) is an important cardiometabolic risk marker in adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D). We estimated the effects of reallocating time among sleep, sedentary behavior, light physical activity (LPA), and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) on six GV outcomes in adults with T1D. Methods: This secondary analysis included 23 adults contributing 102 days with concurrent accelerometer-based activity monitoring and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Compositional rescaling was applied to ensure a 24-h in total. Isotemporal substitution models with linear mixed-effects regression were used to estimate associations of 30-min reallocations among behaviors (e.g., from sleep to LPA) with GV outcomes, including standard deviation of glucose (SD), coefficient of variation (CV), large amplitude of glycemic excursions (LAGE), mean amplitude of glycemic excursions (MAGE), continuous overlapping net glycemic action with a 60-min lag (CONGA-60), and time in range (TIR), while adjusting for covariates. Results: Participants had a mean age of 32.6 years, BMI of 28.2 kg/m2, and diabetes duration of 16.3 years. Reallocating 0.5 hours from sleep to sedentary time, LPA, or MVPA significantly reduced CV (estimate range: -14.4 to -15.2, all p < 0.05) and TIR (estimate range: -3.6 to -3.6, all p < 0.01). Replacing sedentary time with LPA significantly reduced LAGE (estimate = -3.4, p = 0.035). No significant associations were found for SD, MAGE, or CONGA-60. Conclusion: These findings highlight that optimizing glycemic stability in adults with T1D requires a nuanced consideration of how reallocations between sleep, sedentary time, LPA, and MVPA differentially affect GV, TIR, and LAGE.

papers.title: Sedentary behavior as a Gut-Brain metabolic state.
papers.abstract: Sedentary behavior (SB) is prevalent in daily life, with a growing number of studies reporting that higher SB exposure is associated with poorer cardiometabolic and brain health. Thus, in line with a broader paradigm shift, SB should be considered as a postural and low-contractile metabolic state, shaped by both total exposure and bout patterning, that is related to, but distinct from, physical activity (PA), rather than simply the absence of the latter. Regarding the gut microbiome, current evidence on the role of SB remains limited and indirect, as human studies have not yet experimentally manipulated the SB exposure. To generate novel, yet testable hypotheses on the role of SB on the gut microbiome and brain health, this article synthesizes the current evidence base by emphasizing limitations related to cross-sectional designs, measurement heterogeneity, potential confounding by diet, sleep, medications, and PA, and the absence of established quantitative thresholds for SB exposure. Building on broader microbiome, metabolic, inflammatory, and gut-brain axis literature, we outline candidate pathways through which SB exposure, especially prolonged uninterrupted sitting, may alter microbe-derived metabolites and host responses, focusing on short-chain fatty acids, bile acid signaling, and tryptophan-derived metabolism alongside barrier-immune activation and autonomic-vagal circuitry relevant for brain health. Thus, this review extends prior SB-brain health frameworks by positioning SB as a specific gut-brain metabolic state with potential unique effects on a range of brain health-related outcomes. To probe the prediction that changes in SB patterns can affect gut-derived metabolites and specific brain health domains, suitable study designs are discussed. More specifically, future studies should combine accurate measures of SB and PA exposure with gut microbiome and blood-based metabolite assessments, vascular and inflammatory markers, autonomic measures, and standardized tests of cognition and mood, collected at different times, such as after meals and across the day, to better quantify and understand temporal dynamics. Approaching the gut-brain axis by isolating the effects of SB exposure is likely to generate practically relevant and impactful insights that not only help to inform stakeholders, such as policymakers, but also provide the basis for more fine-grained lifestyle recommendations to preserve and improve brain health.

papers.title: The relationship between sleep quality and pain, fatigue, and mood in individuals with lipedema.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThis study aimed to comparatively evaluate sleep quality in individuals with lipedema and healthy controls. In addition, the relationships between sleep quality and depression, anxiety, fatigue, and clinical parameters were investigated.MethodsThis cross-sectional study included 30 women with lipedema and 30 healthy female controls aged 18-75 years. Pain severity in individuals with lipedema was assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS). Lipedema stage, comorbidities, and symptom duration were also recorded. Sleep quality was evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), depressive and anxiety-related symptoms were assessed using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) and Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI), and fatigue severity was evaluated using the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS).ResultsIndividuals with lipedema had significantly higher BDI, BAI, and FSS scores than controls (all p < 0.001 except BDI, p = 0.001). Sleep quality was significantly poorer in the lipedema group (p < 0.001). Among PSQI subcomponents, subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, and daytime dysfunction were significantly worse in individuals with lipedema, while sleep medication use was similar between groups (p > 0.05). In the lipedema group, PSQI scores were positively correlated with depressive (r = 0.489, p = 0.006) and anxiety symptoms (r = 0.386, p = 0.035). No significant associations were found between sleep quality and age, anthropometric measurements, education duration, pain severity, lipedema stage, symptom duration, or fatigue severity.ConclusionsThis study demonstrated poorer sleep quality in individuals with lipedema compared to healthy controls. Sleep quality was also associated with depressive and anxiety-related symptoms, highlighting an association between psychological symptoms and sleep problems in individuals with lipedema.

papers.title: EEG-ECG/HRV associations under multi-stage cognitive stress: characterization and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Mental stress affects cognitive, emotional, and cardiovascular function, but subjective stress scales are susceptible to individual bias. Brain-heart coupling offers a potential approach to stress assessment. This study examined stage-dependent EEG-ECG/HRV associations during mental arithmetic and Stroop tasks. Sixty healthy adults were recruited, EEG and ECG were recorded during baseline rest, four mental-arithmetic stages, inter-task rest, and four Stroop stages. Stage-specific Spearman correlations characterized between-participant associations between five EEG band-power measures and seven ECG/HRV indices. Mixed-effects models separating within- and between-participant effects tested whether within-participant associations varied across difficulty stages and tasks. Significant EEG-HRV correlations decreased in number after task onset and partially recovered during inter-task rest. Mental arithmetic showed more pronounced negative high-frequency EEG-vagal HRV correlations, whereas Stroop showed Theta/Beta-HR associations at onset and sustained Alpha-RMSSD associations during middle-to-late stages. Neither task showed FDR-significant stage-averaged within-participant associations. Within-participant EEG × difficulty-stage interactions were FDR-significant for 12 of 35 whole-frontal associations during mental arithmetic and none during Stroop. Combined models identified five significant within-participant EEG × difficulty × task interactions. No linear difficulty interactions survived FDR correction in sensitivity analyses. These findings support stage-dependent EEG-ECG/HRV associations in this fixed-order cognitive-stress paradigm. They may inform physiologically interpretable candidate measures for objective mental stress assessment and wearable monitoring.

papers.title: Peripheral physiological decoding of arousal in a boundary-avoidance task: signal validity and individualized control.
papers.abstract: Scoring well on a task-demand label does not show that a decoder measures arousal. We ask whether peripheral physiology decodes demand better than EEG, whether the index behaves like graded arousal rather than a clock, and what a controller could do with it.Approach. We re-analysed a public boundary-avoidance flight task in which sixteen participants received EEG neurofeedback, half-sham feedback or silence. A decoder trained on peripheral signals (cardiac, respiratory, electrodermal, pupillometric) from an open-loop calibration block was compared with a retrained EEG decoder, filter-bank common spatial patterns, and motor-only and shuffled-label controls. All analyses are offline; the decoder was never in the loop.Main results. The peripheral decoder reached 93.0% within-subject AUC against 85.2% for EEG. Ring size shrinks on a fixed schedule, so accuracy alone cannot separate arousal from trial position. Three tests did: 48.6% of hard-course trials ended below the scale midpoint; the index separated the courses at matched elapsed time (p= 1.4 ×10-31), where EEG did not; and it tracked the autonomic channels. Only the peripheral index recovered an inverted-U with performance, robust in a duration-safe hazard analysis (p= 3.5 ×10-10). Arousal rose 14.1 points in the 10 s before failure; sustained between-condition differences above 7.5 points are excluded. Subjects varied reliably in how strongly excess arousal predicted failure, predictably from pre-loop calibration. Personalised control bands gave the best held-out discrimination, though at N = 16 indistinguishable from a retuned universal band.Significance. Arousal is a state of the whole body, and here the body reads it better than the scalp. The results separate three often-conflated requirements: accuracy on a demand label, validity as an arousal signal, and usefulness for control. The signal that added information over a fixed rule was distance above a band set by each subject's recent variability.

papers.title: Recovery sleep induces analgesia via sleep ensembles of the zona incerta acting through distinct neural circuits in mice.
papers.abstract: Recovery sleep alleviates pain in humans, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identify a population of sleep-activated neuronal ensembles within the zona incerta (ZI) that mediate both non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and analgesia. Optrode recordings revealed preferential activity of these sleep ensembles during NREM sleep, whereas chronic pain markedly attenuated their activity. Activation of these ensembles increased NREM sleep and reduced pain sensitivity, whereas their inhibition reversed these effects. Gene profiling revealed enriched expression of neurotensin (NTS) within these neurons, and NTS knockdown significantly blunted their sleep-promoting and analgesic functions. Furthermore, ZI sleep ensembles project divergently to the lateral hypothalamus (LH) and the posterior thalamic nucleus (PO). ZI NTS projections to the LH specifically regulate NREM sleep without affecting nociception, whereas projections to the PO selectively mediate analgesia without impacting sleep. Collectively, these findings reveal that ZI sleep ensembles mediate recovery-sleep-induced analgesia, achieving modality specificity through segregated downstream targets.

papers.title: Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise.
papers.abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.

papers.title: Safety and efficacy of high-current tTIS targeting left sgACC for major depressive disorder: A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability, and non-invasive stimulation of deep brain circuits such as the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) remains challenging. This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial recruits 96 adults with moderate-to-severe MDD who received 10 sessions of 2 mA low-current, 15 mA high-current, or sham transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) targeting the left sgACC. The high-current group shows significantly greater reductions in depressive symptoms (17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale [HDRS-17] score) post-treatment and at 1-month follow-up compared with sham and outperforms the low-current group post-treatment. Exploratory Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) analyses suggest improved sleep quality in both active groups, whereas anxiety outcomes show no intergroup differences. High-current tTIS is safe and well tolerated, with only transient tingling. These findings provide preliminary evidence that sgACC-targeted tTIS relieves depressive symptoms safely, with more robust short-to medium-term effects observed under the 15 mA protocol. This trial registers on Chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR2400094971).

papers.title: Sleep Hygiene Intervention for Women Hospitalized during Antepartum.
papers.journal: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing

papers.title: Anxiety and Self-Care in Adolescents with Type 1 Diabetes.
papers.abstract: We aimed to explore the interrelationships among demographic characteristics, sleep quality, diabetes self-care behaviors, and diabetes-specific quality of life among adolescents with type 1 diabetes and anxiety symptoms. We conducted a cross-sectional study in 2024 among adolescents aged 12 to 19 years who had type 1 diabetes for > 6 months, were able to read and speak English, had access to a mobile phone, and had at least mild anxiety symptoms. After informed assent and consent, participants were screened for general anxiety symptoms. If participants had at least mild anxiety symptoms, they completed a demographic survey and measures of sleep quality, diabetes-specific anxiety symptoms, diabetes self-care behaviors, and diabetes-specific quality of life. We calculated descriptive statistics and correlations among continuous measures using Spearman's rho coefficients. Forty adolescents were included in our analysis. They were mostly White (74.36%), non-Hispanic (90%), and female (69.23%). Higher hemoglobin A1c values were significantly associated with lower diabetes self-care scores (p < .001), and lower self-care scores were associated with worse sleep quality (p = .006). Generalized anxiety symptoms were associated with poor sleep (p = 0.012) and diabetes-specific anxiety symptoms were associated with worse diabetes-specific quality of life (p < .001) and worse diabetes self-care (p = .004). Poor sleep quality was associated with worse diabetes-specific quality of life (p < .001). There is a complex interrelationship between psychosocial outcomes and A1c in adolescents with type 1 diabetes and co-occurring anxiety symptoms. Early interventions that address the multi-directional relationship among psychosocial outcomes and A1c among adolescents experiencing type 1 diabetes and anxiety symptoms are critically important to improving self-care behaviors and glycemic control.
papers.journal: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing

papers.title: Longitudinal study of Toba/Qom communities reveals delay and shortening of sleep in real time.
papers.abstract: While artificial light and digital technologies are widely assumed to delay and curtail sleep, direct, longitudinal evidence documenting these changes is remarkably scarce. From 2012 to 2024, we conducted a longitudinal study of native Toba/Qom communities in northern Argentina, including rural groups newly introduced to electricity and semi-urban groups with earlier access to electricity. Using linear mixed-effects models on a dataset of over 12,000 actigraphically recorded sleep events from 156 participants at different times, we observed striking shifts in sleep dynamics. Remarkably, both groups showed delays of close to 1 h in sleep timing, and participants from rural communities lost 35 min of sleep within the course of a decade. These changes occurred across a period that included, first, the introduction of electricity to rural communities after 2016, and, in more recent years, the spread of the internet and smartphone use among the Toba/Qom. While previous work in these and other populations has shown that both factors are associated with changes in sleep habits, our analyses suggest that they cannot fully explain the reported shifts in sleep timing across time by themselves, which may therefore be consistent with concurrent broader processes of modernization and acculturation. These transformations highlight the rapid changes that can take place in communities going through the early stages of the adoption of modern technologies, offering a contemporary parallel to the shifts in human sleep hypothesized to have accompanied global industrialization.

papers.title: Abnormal resting-state EEG microstates correlate with objective sleep parameters in insomnia disorder.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a common sleep disorder, and Electroencephalogram (EEG) microstates, which mirror transient cerebral cortical functional activity, are linked to sleep disorder pathophysiology. The microstate characteristics in insomnia patients and correlations with objective sleep parameters remain to be further explored. This study enrolled 45 insomnia disorder (ID) patients and 48 healthy controls (HC), collecting awake resting-state EEG for microstate analysis; 27 ID and 13 H C participants additionally completed overnight polysomnography (PSG), and exploratory correlation analyses of microstate and PSG data performed for the ID group. Compared with HC, ID patients had markedly shorter duration of microstate A and B, higher occurrence and contribution of microstate C, and reduced duration, occurrence and contribution of microstate D (p < 0.05). ID patients also showed significantly lower transition probabilities of A→D, B→D, D→A and D→B (p < 0.01), and higher probabilities of A→C, B→C, C→A and C→B (p < 0.05). Correlation analyses revealed that in the ID, microstate D occurrence was negatively correlated with rapid eye movement sleep proportion (REM Sleep%, r = -0.427, p = 0.026) and positively correlated with non-rapid eye movement sleep stage 1 proportion (S1%, r = 0.385, p = 0.047). ID patients present significant abnormalities in EEG microstates, and the occurrence of microstate D is correlated with objective sleep indicators of PSG. These findings suggest that EEG microstate parameters may reflect abnormalities in the sleep architecture of ID and may provide references for analyzing the cortical hyperarousal mechanism of chronic insomnia, constructing objective assessment schemes, and developing targeted neuroregulation interventions.

papers.title: Patients with hemispheric epilepsy: Electroclinical characteristics and factors associated with intractability.
papers.abstract: Hemispheric epilepsy has diagnostic and therapeutic challenges and is frequently complicated by drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE). This study aimed to characterize the electroclinical and radiological profile of hemispheric epilepsy and evaluate factors associated with intractability to support individualized management. A retrospective observational study at the Cairo University Epilepsy Unit included 83 patients with a strictly unilateral hemispheric structural lesion on MRI epilepsy protocol, with disease duration ≥ 1 year. All patients had a comprehensive clinical assessment (including QuickDASH), video-EEG evaluation (background, interictal/ictal findings, and concordance), neuroimaging review, and treatment outcome. Logistic regression was used to determine factors associated with DRE. In this cohort, the median age was 22 years (IQR= 14-31) with a near-equal sex distribution. About half had abnormal development, 36% had intellectual disability, and most had mild functional disability. Seizures started at a median age of 9 years (IQR= 4-16). DRE was identified in 54.2%. EEG showed hemispheric slowing in 32.5%. Interictal discharges were ipsilateral in ~75%, and ictal onset (when captured) was ipsilateral in 84.4%. MRI showed mostly left-sided lesions (95%). Etiologies were split between malformations of cortical development (MCDs) -mainly heterotopia/FCD- and acquired (notably post-injury and Rasmussen). Single-domain developmental delay, MCDs, and progressive acquired etiology are associated with DRE (OR ≈7.6, 31.8, and 193.8, respectively). The outcome of hemispheric epilepsy is largely determined by the type of brain lesion, with MCDs and Rasmussen encephalitis conferring the highest risk for intractability. In contrast, static acquired lesions were more often associated with better seizure control.

papers.title: Cross-cohort transfer of clinical Alzheimer's EEG signatures to cognitively healthy APOE-ε4 and PICALM rs3851179 risk carriers using differentiable logic gate networks.
papers.abstract: Neural alterations associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) may emerge years before clinical diagnosis, and genetic risk factors such as APOE-ε4 and PICALM rs3851179 may identify individuals vulnerable to these shifts. We tested whether electroencephalography (EEG) signatures learned from clinically diagnosed AD patients transfer to cognitively healthy middle-aged adults carrying these variants. Differentiable logic gate networks (Diff-Logic) and neural baselines were trained on log-relative power spectral density features from a clinical cohort of AD patients and cognitively normal (CN) controls. These models were then applied without retraining to an independent genetic-risk cohort of neutral-risk non-carriers (N), APOE-ε4-only carriers (A+P-), and dual APOE-ε4/PICALM G-allele carriers (A+P+), yielding a continuous AD-like EEG signature score per participant. Diff-Logic matched neural baselines in clinical classification (balanced accuracy 0.809±0.028; AUROC 0.845±0.023) while enabling edge inference with a 7.4× model-size reduction and 0.22 ms model-only latency on a 7 W single-core CPU. In the genetic-risk cohort, scores were highest in A+P+ participants (0.393±0.167) relative to N (0.296±0.154) and A+P- (0.285±0.143; subject-level mean ± SD). This elevation was nominally significant before correction (A+P+ vs. A+P-, punc=0.036) but did not survive Holm correction (pHolm=0.109), and the cohort carried no AD pathology or conversion ground truth; the association was therefore exploratory. Integrated gradients attribution of the trained model showed genetic-risk relevance in delta, theta, and alpha, partially overlapping clinical AD topography. These findings support the feasibility of zero-shot EEG transfer in genetically at-risk individuals and highlight the need for replication in larger cohorts. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Shyamal-Dharia/ad-difflogic-transfer.

papers.title: Individualized TMS-EEG mapping reveals clinically relevant early prefrontal cortical activity in major depressive disorder.
papers.abstract: To determine whether individualized TMS-EEG mapping improves assessment of early cortical responses in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) compared with conventional Beam F3 targeting and their association with depressive symptom severity. Single-pulse TMS-EEG was performed in 30 patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and 15 healthy controls. Individualized mapping identified DLPFC stimulation sites and intensities that minimized artifacts while eliciting robust early TMS-evoked potentials (>6 μV within 60 ms). Responses were compared with Beam F3 stimulation at 120% resting motor threshold. Early cortical activity was quantified using global mean field power (GMFP) and region-of-interest (ROI) area-under-the-curve (AUC) during the 10-30 ms post-stimulation interval. Individualized mapping produced distinct early cortical responses and significantly smaller early GMFP and ROI AUC responses (q < 0.001) compared to Beam F3 stimulation. Within the MDD group, lower GMFP AUC was associated with greater depression (PHQ-9: ρ = - 0.43, q = 0.046) and anxiety severity (GAD-7: ρ = - 0.58, q = 0.008). Lower ROI AUC was associated with greater depressive symptoms (PHQ-9: ρ = - 0.57, q = 0.008; QIDS-SR: ρ = - 0.48, q = 0.033) and anxiety severity (GAD-7: ρ = - 0.45, q = 0.040). No significant clinical associations were observed for Beam F3-derived measures. Individualized TMS-EEG mapping identifies clinically relevant early DLPFC responses not detected using conventional Beam F3 targeting. Individualized targeting improves the sensitivity of prefrontal TMS-EEG and may enhance detection of early cortical responses associated with depressive and anxiety severity.
papers.journal: Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology

papers.title: Prospective study comparing olfactory function in patients undergoing nasoseptal and rescue flap.
papers.abstract: Endoscopic skull base surgery, whether for treatment or reconstruction, can affect olfaction. Assessing whether the rescue flap technique leads to better olfactory recovery than the nasoseptal flap is essential for developing criteria to guide surgical flap selection. The primary objective of this study was to assess olfactory function in patients undergoing endoscopic skull base surgery with either a nasoseptal or rescue flap. The secondary objective was to evaluate nasal symptoms. Olfactory and nasal symptom assessments were performed using the Connecticut Chemosensory Clinical Research Center (CCCRC) olfactory test and the Sino-nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22) questionnaire at four time points: 24 h preoperatively, and at 1, 3, and 6 months postoperatively. A total of 47 patients were included, divided into two groups: nasoseptal flap (n = 28) and rescue flap (n = 19). Both groups demonstrated preserved olfactory function and site-specific quality-of-life scores when comparing preoperative and 6-month postoperative data. The results indicate that there was no significant change in olfactory function between groups over the evaluated time points, and no long-term deterioration in olfactory function or site-specific quality of life. Neither group demonstrated an earlier olfactory recovery that was statistically significant. Additionally, the SNOT-22 subdomains related to sleep disturbances and psychological symptoms showed progressive improvement, suggesting enhanced sleep quality and improved mental well-being.
authors: Matheus Cunha Ferreira de Castro Tolentino

papers.title: Short-term heart rate variability is associated with seizure outcome in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.
papers.abstract: We examined whether standard 5-minute heart rate variability (HRV) derived from interictal EEG-ECG recordings is associated with postoperative seizure outcome in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). Forty surgical TLE patients were studied before and after resection. Patients with persistent disabling seizures showed greater postoperative reductions in SDNN, RMSSD, LF, and HF power than seizure-free patients after correcting for multiple comparisons. Preoperatively, left TLE was associated with higher heart rate and lower HRV than right TLE, although lateralization differences did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. These findings suggest that cardiac autonomic dysregulation in drug-resistant TLE is associated with postoperative seizure outcome.

papers.title: Does delayed removal of stereo-EEG electrodes following radiofrequency thermocoagulation increase haemorrhage?
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RF-TC) is used in the assessment and treatment of medically refractory epilepsy, typically with electrode removal immediately following ablation. Our SEEG-guided RF-TC protocol includes the option of three further days of recording following thermocoagulation, prior to electrode removal. It is not known whether delayed removal of electrodes following RF-TC may increase the risk of haemorrhage. To compare the rate and volume of intracranial haemorrhage with immediate versus delayed electrode removal following RF-TC. 217 SEEG electrodes from 16 consecutive patients were retrospectively reviewed for haemorrhage. 3D T1-weighted (T1w) and Susceptibility Weighted (SWI) imaging were reviewed for haemorrhage along the electrode tract and at the site of RF-TC. The primary outcome measure was the per-electrode volume of T1w detectable haemorrhage at the site of RF-TC in electrodes removed immediately after RF-TC, compared to electrodes removed 3-days after RF-TC. Secondary outcomes compared the incidence and volume of T1w haemorrhage along the electrode tract in thermocoagulated versus non-thermocoagulated electrodes, presumed due to reflect haemorrhage from electrode insertion/removal. We also describe the temporal evolution of the MRI appearance of haemorrhage following SEEG-guided RF-TC. No clinically significant haemorrhages occurred. At the site of RF-TC a small amount of blood product is universally present but there was no significant difference in per-electrode haemorrhage volume following delayed (93.8 ± 39.8 mm3; ~diameter 5.6 mm) and immediate (80.0 ± 37.5 mm3; ~ diameter 5.3 mm) removal of electrodes (Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.10). At the cortical surface there was no significant difference in the rate of T1w haemorrhage between thermocoagulated and non-thermocoagulated electrodes (63.1% vs 52.5%, p = 0.12, chi-squared). Delayed removal of electrodes post-RF-TC allows assessment of response to RFA and the opportunity for further thermocoagulation if necessary. This exploratory study found no significant increase in haemorrhage volume with delayed electrode removal following RF-TC but a larger study would be required to definitively estimate haemorrhage risk.

papers.title: High accuracy of passive monitoring for detecting hypomanic symptoms in bipolar disorder: an explainable machine learning approach.
papers.abstract: When trying to intervene early to prevent manic episodes, clinicians are hindered by patients underreporting their symptoms as they are becoming hypomanic or manic (i.e., emerging symptoms). Continuous passive monitoring using wearable technology offers a potential solution to address this problem by capturing behavioral signals that do not depend on self-awareness. However, its clinical utility requires validation before implementation. This study aimed to evaluate whether passively collected wearable data can detect hypomanic symptoms using an explainable machine learning framework. We applied explainable machine learning to densely sampled multimodal data from a two-year observational study of digital monitoring in 178 patients with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder (BD) (mean follow-up 540 days; range 120-706 days). Data on activity and sleep were collected continuously using wearable technology. Self-reported data was collected daily on their mood, energy, and anxiety; and weekly using the Altman Self-Rating Mania (ASRM) scale. To identify robust digital markers of hypomanic symptoms, we analyzed 252 time- and frequency-domain features from 43 participants who experienced at least one ASRM-defined symptomatic interval. Passively collected data achieved high accuracy, comparable to daily self-reported data in detecting symptomatic intervals (AU-ROC 0.93 vs 0.91). Combined daily passive wearable data features achieved higher sensitivity (92.0% vs 85.4%) and balanced accuracy (0.90 vs 0.89), and stronger rule-out utility (NPV 97.8% vs 96.1%) than self-report data, with daily sleep features alone driving most of this signal (AU-ROC 0.91; sensitivity 91.8%). The high classification performance using wearable data was explained by reductions in spectral entropy and flux across domains, consistent with decreased complexity and variability in mood, activity, and sleep patterns, consistent with a shift toward pathologically stable states. Passive monitoring using wearable technology can detect hypomanic symptoms with high accuracy, supporting its potential as a clinically meaningful tool for continuous, objective monitoring in patients who underreport hypomanic symptoms. These findings are associative and concurrent in nature; they do not establish predictive validity. Prospective studies are needed to evaluate predictive validity for early detection of ASRM-defined symptomatic intervals.

papers.title: Socially Embedded Digital Coaching Platform to Promote Healthy Lifestyle and Mental Health in Underprivileged (Pre)Pregnant Couples and Young Families (Our Smart Family Buddy Program): Protocol for a Mixed Methods Study.
papers.abstract: The early life course, that is, from preconception up until the first 1000 days of life, is pivotal for optimizing parental and child health. In deprived settings, unfavorable lifestyle behaviors and poor mental health are more prevalent, while access to effective, context-sensitive support is limited. Digital interventions combined with community-based approaches may help address these disparities. This protocol describes the methodology and initial progress of the Our Smart Family Buddy (OSFB) program, which aims to develop, implement, and evaluate a socially embedded digital coaching platform to improve nutrition and mental well-being among (pre)pregnant couples and families in deprived neighborhoods. The OSFB program is a multiphase mixed methods program conducted within a transdisciplinary consortium consisting of 6 interrelated work packages. The program is structured in 3 phases: phase 1, exploration and preparation; phase 2, cocreation, design, and development; and phase 3, prototype evaluation and optimization. Data collection includes quantitative questionnaires, qualitative interviews and focus groups, and digital user data from the platform. The primary outcomes include lifestyle behaviors (nutrition and sleep), mental well-being, user engagement, and implementation outcomes, including feasibility, acceptability, and reach. The program was funded in 2022. A transdisciplinary consortium was established in 2023.
